title: Moonlight and Shadows
description: Moving diagrams bring phases, shadows and orbital geometry to life, from familiar moonlight to the Saros cycle.

questions.prompt: The animation shows the Moon changing appearance. What provides the light on its bright side?
questions.hint: The Moon shines without producing visible light of its own.
questions.explanation: Moonlight is sunlight reflected from the lunar surface.

media.description: Silent scientific animation: a small Moon travels around Earth beside an enlarged view of its face. The visible bright portion changes. Sizes and distances are exaggerated.
media.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio / Ernie Wright, visualization 4158 (2014).

questions.hint: It is close to a calendar month, rather than a week.
questions.explanation: The phase cycle, or synodic month, lasts about 29.5 days.

questions.prompt: If the visible illuminated part of the Moon is getting larger over successive evenings, the Moon is doing what?
questions.hint: The word describes the growing part of the phase cycle.
questions.explanation: Waxing means the illuminated fraction visible from Earth is increasing.

questions.prompt: In the first alignment shown, the Moon passes through Earth's shadow. What event is this?

choices.text: A planetary transit of the Sun

questions.hint: Ask which body is being darkened by the shadow.
questions.explanation: A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.

questions.hint: Their old name reflects how they looked through early telescopes, not what they contain.
questions.explanation: Lunar maria are plains of basalt formed by ancient volcanic lava flows.

questions.prompt: Why does roughly the same lunar hemisphere always face Earth?

choices.text: The Moon's axis always points directly at the Sun
The Moon rotates once per orbit around Earth
The Moon never rotates in space
Earth's clouds conceal the other side

questions.hint: Imagine turning as you walk around something while keeping your face toward it.
questions.explanation: Synchronous rotation makes the Moon's rotation period match its orbital period relative to the stars.

questions.prompt: Why can the Moon appear copper-red during a total lunar eclipse?

choices.text: Earth's atmosphere filters and bends sunlight into the shadow
Lunar rocks suddenly become hot enough to glow
Earth's shadow selectively reflects red light
The Moon's magnetic field produces a red aurora

questions.hint: Some sunlight reaches the Moon after passing through air around Earth's rim.
questions.explanation: Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths more strongly; reddened sunlight refracted into the shadow can illuminate the Moon.

questions.prompt: Why is the Moon's phase cycle longer than its roughly 27.3-day orbit relative to the stars?

choices.text: The Moon stops moving for two days each month
The stars orbit Earth faster than the Moon
The Moon reverses its direction at full Moon
Earth has moved along its orbit, so the Moon must travel farther to regain the Sun–Earth alignment

questions.hint: The phase depends on the Sun's direction, not just the background stars.
questions.explanation: As Earth moves around the Sun, the Moon needs additional orbital motion to return to the same phase geometry.

questions.prompt: The camera changes angle in this animation. What feature explains why most full Moons do not produce an eclipse?

choices.text: The Moon becomes transparent outside eclipse season
The Sun switches off its gravity at full Moon
The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane
Earth casts no shadow during most months

questions.hint: The overhead view hides an important third dimension.
questions.explanation: The lunar orbital plane is tilted about 5 degrees, so the full Moon usually passes above or below Earth's shadow.

media.alt: A changing viewpoint reveals the Moon's orbital plane.
media.description: Silent scientific animation: from above, the Moon appears to meet Earth's shadow; a lower viewing angle shows it missing. Months pass until their paths cross. Earth and Moon are shown at twice their true relative-to-orbit scale.
media.credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio / Ernie Wright, visualization 4158 (2014).

questions.prompt: The Moon rotates fairly uniformly but travels at varying speed in its elliptical orbit. Which observed effect does this help produce?

choices.text: The daily rotation of the entire sky

questions.hint: Rotation and orbital motion do not remain exactly in step at every instant.
questions.explanation: Their changing angular relationship lets us peek slightly around the Moon's eastern and western edges over time.

questions.prompt: All else equal, which change makes an annular solar eclipse more likely than a total one?

choices.text: The Moon being farther from Earth
The Moon being closer to Earth
The observer using a darker filter

questions.hint: Compare the apparent sizes of the Moon and Sun.
questions.explanation: A more distant Moon appears smaller and may not cover the Sun completely, leaving an annulus.

questions.prompt: Using 27.3 days for a prograde moon's sidereal orbit and 365.25 days for its planet's year, which expression gives the phase-cycle period?
questions.hint: The alignment repeats at the difference between two angular frequencies.
questions.explanation: For prograde motion, synodic frequency is lunar orbital frequency minus the planet's orbital frequency; taking its reciprocal gives about 29.5 days.

questions.prompt: A Saros brings similar eclipse geometry back after about 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours. Why is the next solar eclipse in that series usually visible about 120° farther west?

choices.text: The Sun reverses its apparent yearly motion
Earth turns about one third of a revolution during the extra eight hours
The Moon's orbital tilt increases by 120°

questions.hint: The cycle is not a whole number of solar days.
questions.explanation: The extra third of a day lets Earth rotate about 120 degrees. Similar shadow geometry therefore falls at a different longitude, typically westward.
